newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Insurance supervisors set up secretariat at BIS.
newsitem.headline: Insurance supervisors set up secretariat at BIS.

text.p: The International Association of Insurance Supervisors (IAIS), a body of insurance regulators set up two years ago, will establish a permanent secretariat at the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), central bank to the world's central banks.

BIS, which also houses the secretariat of the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision, said in a statement it was pleased to provide a forum in which the growing cooperation among supervisors from the financial sectors can develop.

So far IAIS has not had a formal organisation and the new secretariat in BIS's headquarters in Basle will start out as a small office that will be independent of BIS, which is owned by 32 central banks from around the world.

The decision to locate the secretariat at BIS was influenced by the synergies of being close to Basle Committee banking regulators, by BIS' offer to make office and support facilities available and by the support of the Swiss government, BIS said.
The decision to create a secretariat was taken by IAIS' third annual conference, held in Paris earlier this month.
Setting up a secretariat is IAIS' first step in its plan to become a more substantial association that can speak for insurance supervisors and regulators internationally.

Supervisors from the banking, insurance and securities industry -- the International Organisation of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) -- have gradually been increasing their cooperation in response to the challenges posed by blurring of boundaries between the three segments of the financial industry.

In 1993, for example, representatives from Basle Committee, IAIS and IOSCO formed the Tripartite Group to discuss common issues and develop new tools and techniques to keep up with financial conglomerates that cross traditional lines of banking, insurance and securities.

The first result of the group's discussions was a paper last year that highlighted the risk to the global financial system from the growing number of companies that are taking advantage of deregulation and internationalization of markets to offer a wide range of financial services across the world.

But internationalization of financial markets and conglomerates is not matched by supervisors, who remain bound by national borders and explore issues from their own narrow perspective, leaving a grey area of supervision.
The report proposed appointing lead supervisors, or a convenor, who would be responsible for gathering the information that is necessary to understand the risks assumed by the entire conglomerate.
At their Lyon Summit, the Group of Seven (G7) leading industrial nations also called for enhanced cooperation between financial market regulators.
